title: Caching and Data Freshness
html:
Think about the apps you open many times a day. You reopen a news article on your phone during lunch, or check a product page in a shopping app for the third time before buying. Most of what the app shows you, the headline, the description, the photos, has not changed since your last visit, yet a naive server would read all of it from its database again. A cache stores a copy of a recent result so the server can reuse it, provided the service has a rule for when the stored copy is too old to serve.

Baodium faced that decision during a promotion. Thousands of customers visited a small group of popular product pages, and Catalog Service fetched the same metadata repeatedly from PostgreSQL. The team proposed using Redis to serve recently retrieved values. The change would reduce repeated database reads, although it would also mean that some requests received a copy rather than the latest database record.

Think of a phone number you wrote on a sticky note because you use it often. You can read it in a second, until your colleague changes numbers and the note becomes outdated. Redis offers a similar shortcut. The engineers needed to determine which catalog fields could be cached, how updates would invalidate those copies, and how the database would perform when the cache was empty.

Repeated Reads and Reuse Potential

The affected Product Page Service instance normally handled about 1,200 page requests per second. Each page fetched product metadata, category information, and image references, which came to 3,600 database reads per second, and promotional traffic raised that to about 4,320. Figure Figure shows what repeated reads do to a connection pool.

Those reads shared a pool of 40 connections. During the promotion, short traffic bursts filled the pool and additional requests waited for connections. Chapter 2 provides the capacity calculation. Here the more important decision is which repeated reads can be served from a cache.

Before adding a cache, the engineers looked at which records were being read. Customers requested the same popular products again and again, and descriptions, categories, and image references rarely changed, so a result read for one customer could serve many others.

That combination, many readers asking for the same thing and the thing rarely changing, is where a cache pays off. You will find it on a news site’s front page, in a social network’s profile pages, and in a configuration service read by thousands of processes. A cache does much less when most requests ask for different records, when entries are too large to fit in memory, or when the value changes before anyone else asks for it. A 90 percent hit rate across Baodium’s three kinds of lookup would cut the usual database load from 3,600 reads per second to about 360. When you evaluate a cache proposal, that is the number to focus on, the source reads that will go away.

Measure the hit rate for each kind of data separately. Caching product descriptions does not remove category queries, and a high hit rate for image references tells you nothing about price lookups.

Cache Eligibility and Freshness

Suppose a merchant changes a product description. A customer who sees the old wording for a few minutes can still browse and buy correctly. You cannot assume the same tolerance for every field on the page.

How old a cached value may be depends on what the application does with it. An older description is fine for browsing until the next refresh. An outdated price or permission used to authorize a purchase can lead to a wrong business decision, so those checks must go to a source with the required authority and freshness. A cached inventory figure might show an item as available after another customer has reserved the last unit, and a browsing price might differ from the amount checkout is prepared to charge. The general rule is that the decision a caller makes with a value tells you whether an older copy is acceptable. Table Table applies that rule to the product page.

Cache eligibility depends on how the returned value is used.
Data Cached use Required check
Product description Browsing copy with an accepted update delay. Refresh or invalidate after edits.
Image content Reuse under a content-specific URL. Changed content receives a new URL.
Display price Browsing price under a freshness policy. Validate the purchase price before authorization.
Inventory figure Availability indication while browsing. Reserve through Inventory Service at purchase.
Payment outcome A view of the recorded payment operation. Resolve uncertainty through the owning service.

Price validation also needs a rule for the customer. If checkout finds an updated price, it must show the new amount and get any required confirmation before payment. Otherwise, a correct authoritative read can still produce a purchase the customer did not expect.

Some catalog changes need stricter handling than ordinary edits. Withdrawing a product or restricting access to it may require an authoritative check or a separate update mechanism with a tighter freshness requirement. Giving those controls the same time to live (TTL) as descriptive text, meaning the same period before a cached copy expires, hides an important difference in what can go wrong. Any system that caches permissions faces this distinction, an area where a stale copy can let a revoked user retain access.

Baodium started with browsing metadata, where a delay in showing updates was acceptable. PostgreSQL was still the authoritative store, and checkout continued to use the services responsible for price validation, reservation, and payment.

The Cache-Aside Read Path

The Catalog team chose a shared Redis cache, so that a value loaded by one application instance could be reused by the others. Product Page Service looked in Redis first. If the entry was missing, it read PostgreSQL and stored the result for later callers. Figure Figure traces the path a read takes.

This arrangement is called cache-aside, because the cache sits beside the database rather than in front of it. The application checks the cache, reads the source on a miss, and fills the cache according to its freshness rules.

The code is short, but it hides several decisions. Can another request load the same missing key at the same time? What happens if the cache write fails? Could the database record change between the read and the cache write? The rest of the chapter works through those cases.

Cache Keys and Representations

A cache key identifies the result being reused, so it must include every input that can change that result. If a product description depends on language, a key that contains only the product ID can return the wrong language. If prices depend on currency or customer group, those inputs belong in the price key. And if customer-specific data is stored under a shared key, one customer’s data can be shown to another, which is one of the more embarrassing ways a cache can fail. Authorization checks still apply before you return protected data, even when the value is already in the cache.

The example key includes a representation version, v1. Switching to a new namespace stops a deployment from reading values that earlier code serialized in an incompatible format. It also means that the new namespace starts empty, so the rollout plan has to allow for the extra misses, which can be large, as the section on cold caches shows.

Key design affects invalidation too. When one product has several language or currency variants, an update has to find every cached representation it affects. A key scheme that is easy to build but hard to invalidate only relocates the work to another part of the application.

Cache Placement

Caches can live in several places. A shared cache adds a network call but lets every application instance reuse the same entries. An in-process cache avoids the network call, but each process then has its own contents, its own memory budget, and its own behavior after a restart.

A content delivery network (CDN) suits public content such as product images. Suppose the image URL is derived from the image’s content, for example by including a hash of the file. The old URL then still points to the old image, and an updated page refers to the new URL, so the image itself never needs to be invalidated. This trick, sometimes called cache busting, is how most web applications serve their JavaScript and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) files. The page that contains the image references still needs its own refresh policy.

You can combine these layers, but every extra copy is another place where an old value can be served. A five-minute TTL in the application does not limit the total age of a response that another layer caches afterward. For its first metadata cache, Baodium used only the shared store, which avoided adding another independently refreshed copy in every process. Local caching could come later if measurements showed that particular keys needed it.

Expiration and Freshness Limits

Baodium allowed ordinary browsing metadata to be cached for five minutes. This TTL decides how long an entry can be reused after it is stored. The value itself can be older than that, though, because the TTL clock starts at the cache write, not at the database update.1

Think of a “use within three days of opening” label on a carton of milk. The label says nothing about how long the carton sat in a warehouse before you opened it. A cached value is the same. Suppose a loader reads an older database version, pauses, and then stores the value with a fresh five-minute TTL. The value’s age now includes the pause as well as its time in Redis. Reading from a replica that is behind the primary adds age before the loader even receives the result.

The TTL therefore has to be read alongside the source-read policy. If a value has a strict age requirement, the cache may need the source version, the time it was validated, a limit on how long a loader may run, and a rule for rejecting results that arrive too late.

The TTL also changes the amount of database work. Short TTLs mean more refresh reads, while long TTLs improve reuse but let an outdated entry be served for longer. The product’s freshness requirement and the measured reuse decide where to set it.

Source Updates and Cache Invalidation

Now suppose a merchant changes a description and PostgreSQL commits the new version. Redis may still contain the old description, so the write path has to update or remove that copy. This is the sticky-note problem from the start of the chapter. Figures Figure and Figure show why the write path needs as much thought as the read path.

Updating Redis after the database commit shortens the delay before readers see the new value, but the two writes are separate, the dual-write problem from Chapter 3 in another form. The process can stop between them, and concurrent writers can finish their cache updates out of order.

You have two broad choices. The first is to rely on expiry alone. Readers reload an entry when its TTL runs out, and you avoid having to deliver invalidations or worry about their order. The cost is that the full delay from a source update to a reader seeing it, including the data-age effects described above, must fit within the field’s freshness requirement.

The second choice is to invalidate or update the cache whenever the source changes. In the normal case, readers see the new value soon after the commit, and the delay depends on how soon the invalidation arrives rather than on the TTL. In exchange, correctness now depends on delivery, on the order of concurrent writes, and on what happens when the commit succeeds but the invalidation is lost.

For browsing data with a documented update delay, start with expiry alone and measure the full delay under concurrent updates. If it exceeds the requirement, add invalidation or choose a different read path. Merchants at Baodium expected a corrected price or description to appear on the storefront almost as soon as they saved it, so the team added invalidation and retained the TTL as a backstop in case an invalidation was delayed or lost. Purchase prices, inventory reservations, and permissions still need authoritative checks at the moment of the action, as described in Section Section.

Invalidation removes the cached copy so that the next reader reloads it. That avoids filling the cache with values that may never be requested again, but it requires every path that updates the source to send an invalidation. At Baodium, merchants were not the only writers. Imports, scheduled promotions, supplier feeds, and support tools also changed catalog records, so adding invalidation only to the merchant portal would have left all the other changes waiting for expiry.

The Catalog team recorded an invalidation event with each source update, using the outbox from Chapter 3.

This transaction records the obligation to invalidate, not the invalidation itself, so readers can still get the old copy while the event waits to be published and processed. Every writer has to use this procedure or a change-data-capture mechanism. An outbox inside the Catalog application cannot capture direct database writes made by a separate import tool, whereas change-data capture reads the database’s own change log and captures every committed write, whichever application made it.

The consumer also needs to know which cached entries depend on a change. Changing a product’s category can affect its detail entry and one or more category pages, and invalidating only the detail entry would leave the category pages out of date.

Overlapping Reads and Writes

Even reliable event delivery leaves one gap. Let’s consider a reader whose database result arrives just before a source update. The steps below show what can happen.

  1. A reader misses the cache and reads product version 10.

  2. A writer commits version 11.

  3. The version 11 invalidation removes the cached entry.

  4. The delayed reader stores version 10 with a new TTL.

The invalidation was processed, yet the cache contains the old version again. Deleting a key cannot stop a loader that is already running from writing it back, and on a busy catalog with frequent reads and edits, this ordering is not rare.

Where this race mattered, Baodium stored a minimum accepted source version with each entry, often called a version watermark. Processing the version 11 event raised that minimum to at least 11 and removed any older value. Every write to the cache compared its source version with the minimum and with the version of any existing value, and the write was rejected if it was older. The comparison and the write had to happen atomically, so that a concurrent loader could not slip an older value in between them. In Redis, a short Lua script does this, because the server runs the script as a single operation.

With this rule, the delayed version 10 write is rejected, and a delayed version 10 invalidation event cannot lower the minimum or remove a version 11 value. Every path that writes to the cache must apply the rule, including miss loaders, refreshers, and warmers, because a single unguarded write brings the race back.

The handler that requested the data also has to check the result of its write. If its version 10 value was rejected because version 11 was already known, it can read an acceptable cached copy, make a bounded reload from the source, or return an unavailable result. Returning version 10 anyway would skip the freshness decision for that caller.

Version Metadata and Recovery

The version check prevents one specific failure. It rejects writes that are older than versions the cache already stores. Before the version 11 event arrives, a version 10 write may still be accepted. The version metadata also has to survive for as long as an old loader might still finish. If eviction, expiry, or a restart removes it, an old loader can write into a cache that seems empty.

If your design relies on this protection, define how long the metadata is retained and what happens when the cache is reset. One approach is a cache generation number that each loader reads before it queries the source. After a reset, the generation changes, and writes from loaders that started under the earlier generation are rejected. The generation number itself then needs reliable management.

Use this coordination only where the caller’s freshness policy requires older values to be rejected. Ordinary descriptions can usually tolerate a documented delay, and current purchase decisions are better served by the authoritative price and inventory checks already in place.

Concurrent Misses and Refresh Work

Now consider many concurrent reads of a popular product at the moment its cache entry expires (Figure Figure).

Several requests may see the miss before any loader stores a new value, and each of them then sends the same query to the database. This burst is called a cache stampede, or a thundering herd. It can happen while the overall hit rate is still high, because the hit rate is an average over every key and the stampede involves only one.

The fix is to let callers for the same missing key share one load, which is called request coalescing. Think of an office where the projector stops working in a meeting room. You do not want ten people phoning the help desk. One person calls and tells the others what they learn. Inside a process, the first caller for a key starts the load and the others wait for its result. Go’s golang.org/x/sync package calls this singleflight, the name the helper in this chapter’s code uses. The loader checks the cache once more after it takes responsibility for the key, because another request may have filled it in the meantime.

Waiting callers still need deadlines, and you need to limit how many loaders and waiters can exist concurrently. Otherwise, coalescing reduces duplicate database reads while letting an unbounded number of requests wait, which is the problem from Chapter 4 in a different place. Cancellation needs care as well. One caller leaving the page should not cancel a shared load that other callers are waiting for, so the load needs its own bounded lifetime, separate from each waiter’s deadline.

Coalescing inside each process still leaves some duplication across instances, since twenty processes may each send one read for the same key. If the database can serve that, a shared coordination mechanism may add more complexity than it removes. For expensive loads, instances can coordinate through a refresh lease, which works like the recovery leases from Chapter 3, with an owner token, an expiry, and a release that checks the token. A lease can also expire while its loader is still running, which is why the version checks and database admission still need to be in place.

Expiration Distribution

Coalescing deals with one popular key. A bulk load can cause a different problem by giving thousands of keys nearly the same expiry time. When those entries expire together, many independent loaders reach the database together, like every alarm clock in a building going off at the same minute. Baodium spread the expiry of ordinary metadata across a range below the maximum accepted TTL, a technique known as TTL jitter. The upper end of the range must respect the freshness policy. If the maximum permitted age is five minutes, jitter cannot stretch it to six. Jitter spreads refresh work across keys, but requests for any single expired key still need the coalescing and admission rules described above.

Serving a Copy During Refresh

When the freshness policy permits it, refreshing can begin before the cached copy becomes unusable. Each entry gets a refresh time and a later final expiry. After the refresh time, one loader fetches a new value while other callers go on using the accepted copy. After the final expiry, callers must reload the value or receive a permitted degraded result.

This approach is commonly called stale-while-revalidate, and HTTP supports the same idea through a Cache-Control directive of that name, which many CDNs honor. It suits browsing metadata, because callers do not all have to wait during an ordinary refresh. A failed refresh must not push back the final expiry again and again, though, and the background refresh work needs a limit, especially when many entries reach their refresh time together.

Confirmed Absence and Negative Entries

Requests for products that do not exist can also cause repeated reads. If every request for the same invalid ID reaches PostgreSQL, the application repeats a lookup whose result it already has.

A short-lived negative entry records a confirmed absence, such as NOT_FOUND. It needs a different representation from a cache miss. A source-of-truth lookup can establish that a product does not exist. A timeout cannot. If we cached timeouts as missing products, a brief PostgreSQL outage would turn into false “not found” responses until those entries expired.

Creating or restoring a product must also invalidate or replace any negative entry for it. Otherwise, a newly available product can appear to be missing until the entry expires.

Negative caching helps when callers repeat the same missing IDs. A stream of unique invalid IDs, such as one produced by a scraper or a broken client, still misses every time. Source admission must therefore apply to this path as well.

Decision review

The cache cluster has just failed over

Product Page Service handles about 1,200 page requests per second, and each page needs three catalog reads. The cache was serving 90 percent of them. A failover has left the cache empty but reachable, and PostgreSQL is now receiving close to 3,600 reads per second instead of 360. Acquisition waits are climbing and pages are timing out.

Warm the cache by looping over the most requested products as fast as the loader allows.

Limit how many concurrent misses may reach the database, let the rest wait or fail, and warm a small set first.

Bypass the cache entirely until the incident is over, so reads go straight to PostgreSQL without the extra hop.

C sends every read to the source and gives up the reduction in database reads that recovery depends on. The database receives ten times the rate it was sized for, and the situation lasts until traffic falls.

A is the instinct that turns a cache failure into a database outage. A warmer running flat out competes with live traffic for the same connections, so the queue that live requests are waiting in lengthens while the warmer runs.

B is the recovery this chapter recommends, and the order matters. Limit the database’s concurrency first, so the source survives whatever the cache does. Then warm a small set of popular keys within that limit, because a handful of products account for most reads during a promotion. Requests that cannot be served fall back to a reduced page rather than waiting. The cost is that some customers see an incomplete page for a few minutes, while the admitted requests continue to complete within the tested database allocation.

Cold Caches and Cache Failure

Once most reads are served from the cache, losing those hits changes database demand dramatically. At a 90 percent hit rate, a complete cache outage can send about ten times the usual source-read rate to PostgreSQL. If you sized PostgreSQL for the usual miss rate, a cache outage presents it with a workload ten times larger than the one it was tested for. A cache that was added as an optimization has become part of your capacity plan. Measure whether the database can serve the full rate before you allow unrestricted fallback.

This can happen with every connection healthy. An empty replacement cache, a namespace change, or widespread eviction all produce ordinary misses with the same result. For that reason, the database admission check belongs on every path that reads from the source. If you place it only in the handler for cache errors, all of these other cases go unlimited.

A slow cache needs a short call deadline as well. Without one, a request can spend most of its budget waiting for Redis before it even tries PostgreSQL. During a known outage, the application may skip cache calls for a while, but it must still enforce source admission.

Listings Listing and Listing bring these decisions together in the read path. The helper APIs are illustrative, and they include the population rules described earlier in the chapter.

The first lookup uses the caller’s cache deadline. After a miss, the singleflight.run function shares one loader among concurrent requests for the same key. The loader checks the cache again before using any database capacity.

The cache helpers return distinct results for missing entries, unavailable cache access, and rejected writes, so the caller never has to guess which happened. A failed cache write does not undo a successful source read, so that result can still be returned. A version rejection means that newer data is already known, which needs separate handling, and this example returns temporary unavailability instead of starting another read.

The database permit covers the source operation through local cleanup, as in Chapter 4. Warmers, refreshers, and verification reads use the same source allocation instead of each getting their own allowance against the same database. As with every per-instance limit you have seen so far, the combined allocation has to fit within the local connection pools and the database’s capacity across the whole fleet, including the extra instances that run during a rollout.

Warming and Recovery

A shared cache survives when one application instance restarts. Warming matters after a cache reset, a namespace change, or the creation of a separate local cache.

Baodium warmed a selected set of frequently requested keys at a limited rate. Loading the entire catalog would have used database reads and memory for products that might never be requested. The warmers shared the source allowance with live misses, could be paused when customer requests needed that capacity, and gave their entries spread-out expiry times. The recovery test ran warming and live requests together, because filling the cache as fast as possible could have recreated the database overload the cache was meant to prevent.

Field note

Facebook, September 2010

Facebook’s September 2010 outage lasted about two and a half hours. An automated system for verifying configuration values treated a changed value in the persistent store as invalid. Every client that read the value tried to repair it by querying a cluster of databases, which soon received hundreds of thousands of queries per second. Clients then treated database errors as invalid values and deleted the corresponding cache entries, which produced still more queries, even after the original value had been corrected.

Engineers stopped all traffic to the database cluster, disabled the verification system, and let traffic back in gradually. A repair path needs admission control just as much as an ordinary cache-miss path does, and an error from the source is no reason to treat a cached value as invalid.

Source: published incident report.

Cache Memory and Hot Keys

A cache can be up and responding to every request while removing very few reads from the database, because entries are evicted before their TTL runs out. When memory fills, the eviction policy decides which entries go. A policy based on recent access reacts well to changing demand, but a scan through the catalog can fill the cache with records that are used once. A policy based on access frequency retains established popular entries but reacts more slowly to a new promotion. In Redis, these correspond to settings such as allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu. If you run Redis yourself, check the maxmemory-policy setting. Its default, noeviction, makes writes fail when memory is full instead of evicting anything.

Test the policy against your application’s access pattern. The source-read rate, hit rate, eviction rate, and memory use tell you far more than the policy name. When you estimate memory, include the serialized payloads and the per-entry overhead. Caching an entire product response when callers use only a small part of it wastes both memory and transfer time.

A single popular key can also concentrate requests on the shard that owns it. Adding shards does not spread that key’s reads, so check per-shard measurements even when the cache’s overall numbers are good. A small local cache in each process can reduce network reads for such a key, provided its freshness policy allows another copy. That is a measured extension to the design, with its own expiry and invalidation requirements.

Cache Validation and Telemetry

The release tests had to show two things, how much source work the cache avoided and whether the copies it returned were suitable for their intended use.

For the read path, the engineers tested an empty cache, a cache that timed out, concurrent requests for an expired product, and many entries expiring together. Source admission had to apply in every case, including when Redis returned ordinary misses.

For the write path, they paused a loader after it read an old version, committed a source update, processed the invalidation, and then let the loader finish. This reproduced the race that a sequential read-and-write test would miss. They also tested delayed invalidation, cache resets during loading, product creation after a negative entry, and recovery while customers continued browsing.

In production, the rate of source reads showed how much database work was still happening. Hit rate by route and data class showed where reuse was effective, and the numbers of coalesced requests, refreshes, and admission rejections explained what happened after misses. Cache latency, errors, memory, and evictions were measured per shard.

Invalidation lag and sampled comparisons between cached and source versions provided evidence about freshness. The sampling itself used a limited share of the database allocation. A difference shortly after an update could be within the freshness policy, so the number of mismatches alone did not prove a defect. Repairs also needed concurrency protection. A verifier that found an old entry could not blindly delete the key, because another caller might have written a newer value in the meantime, so repairs used a conditional version check or the normal invalidation procedure.

Finally, the page response distinguished absence from unavailability. Optional metadata could be left out after an admission rejection, a “product not found” result required confirmed absence, and checkout still obtained its authoritative decisions for the purchase.

Configuration Versions and Cache Freshness

Caching shows up again in a place many teams do not think of as a cache. At Baodium, about 500 application instances read feature flags, rate limits, and policy rules from a shared configuration service. Administrators change configuration through that one authoritative service, and every instance needs to discover new revisions without querying its database on every request.

The trick is to separate the part that never changes from the part that does. Once a configuration revision is published, its contents are frozen, so revision 18 means the same thing forever. The publisher writes the new revision and, in the same transaction, updates a pointer that says which revision is active. An instance fetches a revision’s contents by number, checks the digest, and can cache those contents for as long as that revision is in use, because they will never change. Only the pointer needs a freshness rule, since that is the one thing an administrator can change.

How long does a change take to reach every instance? If instances check the pointer once a minute, a change can take up to a minute to arrive, plus a little network and processing time. A push notification shortens that, but notifications get dropped and connections reconnect, so each instance still checks the pointer on a schedule as a safety net. And the notification itself should carry only the news, “revision 18 is available.” The instance then fetches and verifies revision 18 from the authoritative service, rather than trusting whatever arrived in the message.

Not every setting deserves the same care. A dashboard color scheme can safely be a few minutes old. A deployment permission that was just revoked cannot, so the endpoint that enforces it checks the current authoritative revision before acting. If the configuration service is unreachable at that moment, the endpoint reports that it cannot decide, rather than falling back on a cached approval that may no longer be valid.

For storage, PostgreSQL handles publication and the pointer comfortably at this scale. Redis earns a place only if so many instances fetch the same revision concurrently that local caches cannot serve the load. As always, the choice comes from the consistency promise, how often configuration changes, and the peak read rate. Chapter 10 returns to the release rules for changes whose effects must be evaluated gradually.

Summary

Caching is one of the few changes that can remove most of a database’s load in an afternoon, which is the very reason it deserves care. The question to ask is not whether a value can be cached, but what the caller will do with it. A product description that is a few minutes old will not change what a customer buys. An old price, permission, or stock level can, and those values need an authoritative check no matter how good the cache is.

Once that decision is made, the rest of the chapter is about the moments when a cache stops helping. A read that overlaps an update can put an old value back. Many requests for one expired key can all reach the database in the same moment. A restart or failover can empty the cache and send the full load to a database that was sized for the misses. Version checks, coalesced loading, staggered expiry, and admission on every miss path are the tools for those moments. A useful habit is to ask, for any cache you add, how the database would cope if the cache were empty right now.

Caching made Catalog cheaper to run, but the next problem had nothing to do with data. The same application revision worked on some hosts and failed on others, which is where Chapter 6 begins.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The selected browsing data permits a defined update delay, and reusing frequently requested records reduces source reads by the measured hit rate.
Condition that tests it & A popular entry expires, an invalidation is missed, or the cache becomes unavailable.
Constraint or invariant & Cache calls, concurrent loaders, database connections, and source-read admission have separate limits. Live misses, refreshers, warmers, and verification share the database allocation.
Evidence and uncertainty & The usual product-page workload generated 3

,
600 database reads per second per affected instance. A 90 percent hit rate across those lookups would reduce source reads to about 360 per second, before refresh and verification work.

Still unknown: the miss rate during expiry, eviction, or cache loss, and whether delayed writes can break the accepted freshness policy after updates or cache resets.

Signal and evaluation window & During cache-loss and refresh tests, measure source-read concurrency, cached-value age, and acquisition time.
Control and decision & Use cached copies under their freshness policy and apply source admission to every miss path. Distinguish missing data from unavailable data, and validate purchase decisions through their authoritative services.
Owner and review trigger & The Catalog owner defines cache eligibility and update handling. The service and database owners agree on source-read admission and recovery capacity. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.

  1. Redis may remove expired keys through lazy and active expiration. The application should treat an expired key as unavailable even if the physical entry has not yet been reclaimed.↩︎
